title: How the rightwing operative David Horowitz shaped Stephen Miller | Sidney Blumenthal
text:
Stephen Miller has risen to the top of the White House in the downdraft of Donald Trump’s abject defeat in the midterm elections. It is no irony to Trump that he has elevated Miller as his ideal bullying enforcer only after Trump’s own thorough repudiation. Appointing Miller is Trump’s denial that he is the worst thing he could possibly imagine: a loser.
Trump has no more time for adults in the room who might want to negotiate with the new powers-that-be in the Congress. He has searched his soul, as he explained in his interview on 60 Minutes, entertaining his wish to ascend to heaven.
“I don’t want to go to hell,” he said. He must be true to himself. Asked about “forgiveness” of his critics, Trump disparaged “forgiveness”. “I can use the word hate, I do hate some of my enemies. I think they’re – they’ve been terrible. Look what they’ve put me through, the weaponization. I got indicted–” Trump is the eternal victim in a world of “enemies”.
Miller’s superiority complex neatly complements Trump’s malignant narcissism. Trump is Miller’s calling; Trumpism is his profession. His life has led to this consummation. Miller feels most superior, most himself, servicing Trump’s megalomania.
Miller is far more than a yes-man extraordinaire. Miles Taylor, the chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security in the first Trump term, recalls being present when, after a lower federal court decision went against the administration, Trump banged his desk. “We need to get rid of the judges,” he reportedly said. In Taylor’s account, Miller piped up: “Yes sir, a country without judges would help.”
Miller projects his superiority complex as more than the lament of the lonely truth-teller. He debases opponents as “dumb”, “stupid”, “ignorant” and“foolish”. He construes every issue as Manichean, zero-sum and existential. Those who disagree with him are not only illegitimate but also threaten the survival of the nation. “If it wasn’t for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now. This man saved America,” he said this month.
Miller’s technique of vicious denigration denies that his opponents have any credibility without ever engaging their arguments. His absolutism wraps him in total authority in order to intimidate and dominate any discussion. His vehemence signals he is fighting a righteous crusade against nefarious enemies, from “wokeism” to “diversity” to the “deep state”.
Miller’s sophistry echoes the “great replacement theory”, still another expression of his superiority complex, which recycles white nationalist tropes. He is a fan of the 1973 neo-fascist, racist novel The Camp of the Saints, in which third-world masses invade a decadent Europe.
Miller uses the word “invasion” routinely to characterize immigration. “We are being conquered,” Miller has said. “This is a complete resettlement of America in real time … a generation from now … people will not know the country that they are living in.”
He is the prime mover behind Trump’s challenge to birthright citizenship in the 14th amendment. Once again, Miller uses the word “invasion”: birthright citizenship is “the biggest, costliest scam in financial history … it is the number one magnet for illegal immigration and invasion.”
The omnipotent Trump is yet another of Miller’s projections of superiority. “The powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned,” Miller said. His fuhrerprinzip inferentially includes the leader’s shadow, Miller himself, who also “will not be questioned”.
Miller’s fanaticism has its sources in obvious rightwing motivation, but in his case his tutelage took place under an unusual mentor in the Bolshevik style of invective. If ever there is a classic contemporary example of status anxiety as the origin of radical right resentment, it is that of Stephen Miller.
Miller’s father, a real estate investor, lost money, and the family moved from a luxurious home in Santa Monica to a smaller one in a more diverse neighborhood. Instead of attending a private school, Stephen went to Santa Monica High, highly ranked with a large Latino student presence.
“Hi, I’m Stephen Miller, some of you may or may not know who I am,” Miller said to an assembly when he ran for the student council. “I’m the only candidate up here who stands out … Am I the only one who is sick and tired of being told to pick up our trash when we have plenty of janitors who are paid to do it for us?”
Miller cut ties to a childhood friend, Jason Islas, according to Islas, “because I am Latino”. Miller chose a quote for his yearbook to highlight his opposition to multicultural events at the school: “There can be no fifty-fifty Americanism in this country.”
Miller began calling into a local rightwing talk radio show to denounce students and teachers for “stupidity”. According to Miller’s biographer, Jean Guerrero, he took the initiative to reach out to the best known and most provocative rightwing operative residing in Los Angeles to invite him to speak to the school.
By then, David Horowitz was at the head of a far-right empire of magazines, books and organizations funded to the tune of more than $50m. His publications were filled with vicious personal attacks, particularly on feminist academics, one of whom was depicted in a crude graphic with full frontal nudity as “Ms April”. He would call his chief organization the David Horowitz Freedom Center: A School for Political Warfare, its role as that of “a battle tank” against the “political left” an “existential threat”.
Horowitz was a volatile, brooding Dostoyevskyian character, born and raised in a Communist party family with Stalin as the household god. Horowitz was possessed of considerable intellectual gifts, which he deranged and squandered.
After writing a Marxist critique of US imperialism, he became an editor at Ramparts magazine, a freewheeling New Left publication in San Francisco. Another editor, Richard Parker, who later became a Harvard professor, recalled opening a closet door in the office and almost being buried by thick books tumbling out.
They were the Collected Works of Kim Jung Il, the North Korean dictator. Parker asked Horowitz if he knew anything about this. Horowitz replied that he thought they would make good premiums for subscribers. Parker decided Horowitz was “psychotic”.
Horowitz became a camp follower of the Black Panthers in nearby Oakland and was enamored of their leader Huey P Newton as the vanguard of the revolution. Though friends warned against it, Horowitz recommended an acquaintance, Betty Van Patter, to be their bookkeeper. After her mysterious death in suspicious circumstances – a case that remains unsolved – his politics shifted.
“In my mind, you are the person responsible for her death,” the radical journalist and Horowitz friend, Art Goldberg, wrote him. “I distinctly remember warning you to be careful about getting too involved with the Panthers because things were getting pretty crazy at the time you jumped in …. The problem was that you were inexperienced and naive and Betty Van Patter got killed because of it.” Horowitz replied that this was Goldberg’s “alibi”, “about blaming everyone but yourselves”, and “it shows me what wretched human beings I was involved with when I was one of you – when I was a member of the progressive vanguard.”
Horowitz developed a mythology of his disillusionment. He absolved his personal guilt, shifted the blame to “the left”, and used the murder as the epiphany for his political conversion. He turned his negligence into his story of his awakening.
Horowitz flipped from far left to far right but was completely unchanged in his Leninist tactics and apocalyptic mindset. “Politics is war: Don’t forget it,” he wrote in his 1999 book, The Art of Political War: How Republicans Can Fight to Win.
Now, in charge of a lucrative rightwing operation, Horowitz took on Miller as his protege. Horowitz also mentored Charlie Kirk, who called him “a titan in the battle of ideas”, bankrolled the Islamophobe Robert Spencer, allied with the then unknown Stephen Bannon, and promoted the rise of Ron DeSantis.
After Miller graduated from Duke, where he used the Horowitz front group, Students for Academic Freedom, to attack multiculturalism and liberalism as the campus crank, Horowitz secured for him a series of jobs, first as press secretary for the representative Michelle Bachmann, of Minnesota, a Tea Party radical, and then with the senator Jeff Sessions, of Alabama.
Miller was an eager receptacle for Horowitz’s core ideas and tactics – of total political warfare against the evil enemy within of mainstream institutions, from the media to the universities to government agencies; and that immigration is an elemental multicultural threat to civilization.
Virtually every notion and formulation Miller advanced came from Horowitz, who remained close to him into the second Trump term, until he died in 2025, upon which Miller got Trump to tape a memorial video tribute to Horowitz as “a great patriot”.
Just as Trump was the protege of Roy Cohn, Miller was the protege of David Horowitz. But Trump had his own experience apart from Cohn in a variety of worlds and demimondes. Miller, however, was Horowitz’s test-tube experiment, his mimetic creation, a kind of homunculus, a mini-me.
Cohn was a liar, a thief and a scoundrel, but he was not a convert. He had his own independent and expansive social and political base in New York. Highly influential people who were not conservatives embraced him because he was useful and amusing. If Cohn had dropped Trump as a client, or Trump dropped him, Cohn’s influence and wealth would have been unimpaired.
Miller, by contrast, has no independent existence apart from Trump. He is as disposable as his inner circle of administration staffers and hangers-on. He is universally loathed, which he takes as a sign of his superiority, but though being the focus of such hatred commends him to Trump, it cannot substitute for a constituency.
He may be Trump’s retribution, but he’s also an appendage. Miller is fated for the bunker, to accelerate the pyrotechnics of Trump’s final act, his Gotterdammerung.
- Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast
